problem: Prior VLN methods either need fine-tuning on large data or, when zero-shot, rely on exhaustive exploration, weak task decomposition and many costly VLM queries, so they generalize poorly and are slow in unseen environments.
motivation: Real-world deployment needs rapid adaptation to new buildings without retraining. The paper observes that a VLM can build a compact top-down scene graph from a short exploration, and that a planner reasoning over this map can reuse validated route segments to cut VLM calls and latency.
key_idea: Use a VLM to explore an unseen environment within a 1-hour budget to build a top-down scene graph map, then run a zero-shot VLM planner over the map with a hierarchical trajectory cache that reuses validated task/subtask routes.
insight: Giving the VLM a symbolic top-down map (with the current pose and trajectory) instead of only first-person views lifts zero-shot SR well above prior zero-shot methods. The caching experiment shows reuse of subtask trajectories cuts VLM calls by up to 78.6% and time by up to 78.8%. Note the map is built from a pre-exploration phase, which is not free in comparison to other zero-shot baselines, and there are no ablations of the exploration prompt or map.
method: VLM-guided exploration: at each step GPT-4.1 receives constraints, the current scene graph and the first-person RGB, and outputs one of four actions (forward, left, right, stop) using a prompt that discourages revisits and unsafe moves.
Scene graph construction: partial graphs from each step are merged into a global top-down map built with IMU odometry, with semantic room tags (e.g. kitchen, living room).
Coverage stopping criterion: exploration ends at the 1 hour limit or when the map periphery forms a closed loop and there are no large unexplored empty regions.

Neurosymbolic planner: P(Φ, o, T_p, G_S) prompts the VLM with the top-down map (start square, pose arrow, trajectory, navigable/obstacle areas), the current view and the constraints, and outputs a discrete action.
Task decomposition: the VLM decomposes the task prompt into subtasks/location-specific queries such as room-to-room or object-to-object transitions.

Hierarchical cache: a dictionary maps (task, location) to trajectories at task, subtask and fragment levels; lookup goes task-level, then subtask-level, then falls back to VLM planning and stores the new trajectory.
Real-robot deployment: a Unitree Go2 with a RealSense D456 builds the map using ORB-SLAM and LIO odometry.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 (frozen, API); GPT-5 also shown qualitatively
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB + odometry (IMU); RealSense depth on the real robot
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move forward, turn left, turn right, stop
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration of each test environment (up to 1 hour) to build a top-down scene graph map before deployment; instructions are not used.

numbers.extra: Uses pre-explored top-down scene graph (1 hour exploration) and odometry; does not use the instruction text.
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Cross-dataset performance on R2R Val-Unseen): VLN-Zero 5.97 / 51.6 / 42.4 / 26.3

numbers.extra: Uses pre-explored top-down scene graph and odometry; does not use the instruction text.

numbers_note: Caching results (Table 2) are for two episodes in one scene, e.g. episode 1691: VLM calls 84 -> 18, total time 167.605 s -> 35.500 s; they are not benchmark metrics.
results: On R2R-CE val-unseen, VLN-Zero reaches SR 42.4 and SPL 26.3 versus the best zero-shot baseline CA-Nav at SR 25.3 and SPL 10.8 (Open-Nav SPL 12.9). On RxR-CE SR is 30.8 versus AO-Planner at 22.4, and it is competitive with several fine-tuned models (e.g. it beats NaVid on R2R SR 37.0 but is below NaVILA at 54.0). Caching cuts VLM calls by up to 78.6% and time by up to 78.8% on selected episodes.
limitations: Requires a pre-exploration phase (up to 1 hour) to build the map, and the comparison with zero-shot baselines that do not have this map is not like-for-like; evaluation ignores the instruction text.
Caching evaluated only on two episodes in one scene; no ablations of the exploration prompt or scene graph, and the real-robot demo is a single small apartment.
Assumes complete, static maps and indoor scenes; partially observed or dynamic environments are left to future work.
